headline: High: AutoGPT can write and execute shell commands while the other agent has no documented isolation, creating dangerous interaction and conflict risks; prompt-injection and leakage are less evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can produce agentic content in an MCP/RAG-oriented repo, while Agent B can consume filesystem and agent-protocol inputs and execute shell commands. No shared channel is documented, so the pathway is inferred rather than proven; uncertainty pushes this above low. The interaction could let attacker-controlled content from A steer B if bridged manually or via files.
conditions: IF Agent A outputs instructions into a file or message that Agent B reads as trusted input, injection is possible.
IF an orchestrator bridges A to B through filesystem or agent protocol without provenance checks, prompt injection can propagate.
mitigations: Add a provenance label to every A output before B reads it.
Require B to ignore instruction-like text inside A outputs.
Use a separate staging file for A outputs and review it manually.
Disable automatic file-to-prompt ingestion between the agents.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A has network egress none, so it is not a likely exfiltration source. B has allowlisted egress and filesystem access, but neither profile shows sensitive data classes or a shared workspace. The pairwise leakage path is therefore possible only through external orchestration or manual transfer, making the blast radius small and the evidence weak.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same local workspace, file contents could move between them.
IF the operator copies A outputs into B inputs, any embedded data can be relayed onward.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate directories.
Avoid copying raw outputs from A into B.
Review B's allowlisted destinations before enabling runs.
Store sensitive files outside any shared workspace.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses, and it has filesystem access; A is an agentic repo with MCP/RAG tags but no explicit write surface is documented. Because A's write capability is not stated, I cannot assume it is absent or present; uncertainty escalates the conflict risk to medium rather than low. If both touch the same files, conflicts are plausible.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write into the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF B runs shell commands that modify repo state while A also edits files, conflicts can arise.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Disable write access for one agent during the other's run.
Use git branches per agent.
Check for file locks before writes.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B's agentic shell and filesystem access make it plausible that it will act on A's outputs if the orchestrator wires them together. A is an agentic/RAG-oriented repo, so it may emit synthesized facts or instructions; B can then operationalize them. No verification step is documented, so the cascade is inferred and medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF B treats A's output as authoritative input, downstream actions can follow incorrect content.
IF A-generated text is passed into B without a verification step, errors can cascade into shell actions.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between A and B.
Require B to cite source files before acting.
Limit B to read-only mode for A outputs.
Log every A-to-B handoff for audit.
requires-engineering: add automated verification of A outputs before B acts.

E_compliance.rationale: Neither profile documents regulated data classes, residency constraints, certifications, or retention differences. A has no touched data classes and B likewise lists none, so there is no evidenced compliance mismatch to assess. The other agent is cited only to show the pair lacks a documented compliance pathway.
conditions: IF either profile later documents regulated data classes or residency constraints, reassess compliance risk.
IF the deployment introduces PHI, EU PII, or secrets handling, compliance analysis changes.
mitigations: Document data classes before deployment.
Confirm residency requirements for any future data.
Review retention settings if sensitive data is added.
Keep secrets handling disabled unless required.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated data classes.
